problem: The lens-hedge pattern is `"(?i)(-like|like a|likeness|reminiscent|approximat|similar to)"`. JSON Schema mandates ECMA-262 regex, which has no inline `(?i)` flag: `new RegExp("(?i)(...)")` throws `Invalid regular expression ... Invalid group`. ajv therefore refuses to compile taxonomy-node.schema.json, and because every other schema `$ref`s it (`https://schema.uvrc.dev/v1/taxonomy-node.schema.json#/$defs/...`), ALL SEVEN schemas become uncompilable in any JS/ajv toolchain. INV-TAX-3 (the lens honesty rule the brief calls non-negotiable) is consequently unenforced, and tests/validate-taxonomy.mjs does not check prompt_fragment hedging either — only the `_like` id suffix. README.md:78 ("7 JSON Schemas ... all meta-valid") and DATA_SCHEMA.md:1957 ("All seven schema files pass Draft202012Validator.check_schema") are both true only under Python's `re`, which accepts a leading `(?i)`; the Python-only validation masked the defect.
fix: Replace the pattern with an ECMA-262-legal alternation covering both cases, e.g. `"([Ll]ike|-like|likeness|[Rr]eminiscent|[Aa]pproximat|similar to)"`, or move the case-insensitive check into tests/validate-taxonomy.mjs and keep only a case-sensitive pattern in the schema. Then add a CI step that compiles all seven schemas with ajv (not only Python jsonschema) so an ECMA-illegal regex can never land again.
evidence: $ node -e "new RegExp('(?i)(-like|like a|...)')" -> THROWS: Invalid regular expression: Invalid group. Loading all 7 schemas into ajv 2020 fails until this one pattern is patched; after patching, all 740 taxonomy nodes validate clean.

Both paths send genuinely free, correctly-labelled CC BY / CC BY-SA content into a manual queue.

Whether an attribution obligation is discharged by UI adjacency — when the artefact the user actually copies and pastes elsewhere is deliberately stripped of all credit — is a legal question about the licence's attribution term, not an engineering one. The document's own front-matter disclaimer promises that 'Where a question is genuinely legal rather than technical, this document says so, marks it `(UNVERIFIED — legal question)`, and takes the conservative branch rather than guessing.' Here it does the opposite: it makes the legal call and takes the *less* conservative branch, and the sentence reads as legal advice to any downstream reader.
fix: Reword to describe behaviour, not legal effect: 'The prompt text carries no attribution; the notice travels beside it in a persistent, non-dismissible References-used panel and in every file export. `(UNVERIFIED — legal question: whether an on-screen notice discharges the attribution term when only the prompt text leaves the app.)`' Additionally add a conservative fallback the doc can commit to now — e.g. the clipboard write also places a plain-text attribution block on the clipboard as a second flavour, or copying is disabled-by-default for mixes whose `license_summary.requires_attribution` is true — and record the choice as a policy decision rather than a legal conclusion.

location: LP-2 (line 62) together with LP-11 (line 126) and the LP-9 user-facing notice (line 111)
problem: LP-2 states as structural fact that 'The product **points at** media; it does not incorporate it… the moment we stored a byte of the media in the repository, this separation would become an argument instead of a fact.' Whether hot-linking / embedding a third-party image into your own UI is 'not incorporating it' is a genuinely contested legal question (the inline-linking / server-test line of cases is not settled and has gone the other way in some US courts on the public display right), and it varies by jurisdiction. This unmarked legal conclusion is load-bearing for the riskiest behaviour in the whole product: LP-11 explicitly permits *displaying* references whose licence is `excluded` — i.e. rendering hot-linked CC BY-NC, `proprietary` and `unknown`-licence media in the UI with a red badge. Separately, the LP-9 warning shown verbatim to end users asserts 'This tool does not redistribute the image' — a legal characterisation stated flatly in user-facing copy, where the doc-level 'not legal advice' disclaimer is not visible.
fix: (1) In LP-2, mark the claim: 'The product points at media rather than storing it. `(UNVERIFIED — legal question: whether embedding a remote image constitutes a display or reproduction is jurisdiction-dependent; the no-binaries rule is our conservative engineering branch, not a legal conclusion.)`' (2) In LP-11, narrow the affordance: render *counts and licence labels* for excluded results by default and gate the thumbnail behind an explicit operator setting, or render the provider's own server-side thumbnail only. State the reason. (3) In the LP-9 verbatim notice, delete 'This tool does not redistribute the image and' and keep the hedged remainder, so no user-facing string asserts a legal characterisation.
